boxbrown: This man climbed inside a wooden box... and paid someone to mail him hundreds of miles away.
The box was three feet long. He was five foot eight.
He had a little water... and a few tiny holes for air.
The label said: This side up, with care.
Twice, it was turned upside down.
Once, for an hour and a half. His eyes swelled until he thought they'd burst... and he didn't make a sound.
Then two workers flipped the box on its side, and sat on it.
So why would a man mail himself?
Because Henry Brown was enslaved in Virginia, and his wife and children had just been sold away.
He paid eighty-six dollars, more than half his savings, to be shipped north as dry goods.
Wagon. Train. Steamboat. Ferry. Twenty-seven hours.
In Philadelphia, abolitionists pried the lid open...
and the man who'd been mailed like a package stood up... free.
From then on, the world called him Henry Box Brown.
bridge: These soldiers were marching perfectly together... until their footsteps started destroying the bridge beneath them.
With every step, the deck dipped. Then bounced back. Then dipped again.
England, eighteen thirty-one. About seventy riflemen, four abreast, on an iron chain bridge.
Then... a crack. One end of the bridge collapsed, and dozens of men fell into the river.
But how can walking break an iron bridge?
You see, a bridge is a bit like a swing.
Push it at random, and nothing happens. Push it on the same beat, again and again, and it swings higher and higher.
Seventy men stepping together were pushing the bridge on one beat.
Investigators found a badly made bolt had snapped. It might have failed anyway... but the marching sped it up.
No one was killed, but twenty men were injured.
And the army gave a new order: when you cross a bridge... break step.
That's why some old bridges still carry signs telling soldiers to break step.
canary: These miners carried tiny birds underground... and some even had emergency oxygen tanks for them.
A metal box. A glass window. A little round door. And on top, an oxygen cylinder.
Why would a bird need its own oxygen?
Because down here, the deadliest danger has no smell, no color, and no taste.
Carbon monoxide. After explosions and fires, it filled the tunnels... and miners couldn't tell.
In eighteen ninety-six, scientist John Haldane found carbon monoxide behind a deadly Welsh mine explosion.
His idea? Send a small animal first.
You see, a canary breathes fast, so the gas hits its tiny body long before a person's.
If the bird wobbled, or dropped from its perch... everyone got out.
But rescue teams had a better cage.
When the bird collapsed, they shut the little door... and opened the valve.
Oxygen flooded in... and the canary could be brought back.
British mines kept canaries on the job until nineteen eighty-six.
